title: Breast Cancer Prevention and Treatment: Misinformation on Pinterest, 2018
screen_reason: Hand-coded content analysis of 797 Pinterest pins retrieved by breast-cancer keyword searches. Reports the share of items classified as containing misinformation, judged against external authoritative sources (Memorial Sloan Kettering, World Cancer Research Fund, National Cancer Institute, BreastCancer.org, Susan G. Komen, published academic papers), with an explicit denominator. This is a CONTENT prevalence estimate, not a quality-scale study.

estimates.country: Not stated (Pinterest platform-wide; authors based in the USA and framed around US women)
estimates.measure_type: % of all breast-cancer-related Pinterest pins retrieved that contained misinformation about breast cancer prevention or treatment
estimates.value_raw: 91 of 797 pins (11.4% of the sample overall); 178 (22.3%) of 797 made a factual claim, of which 91 (51.1%) contained misinformation
estimates.denominator: 797 Pinterest pins retrieved by six searches on the terms "breast cancer" and "breast + cancer" (838 scraped, 41 dead links discarded)
estimates.definition: A pin was coded as containing misinformation if at least one claim in its text or image was shown to be false by evidence from reputable breast-cancer information sources; only one false claim was required
estimates.misinfo_def: "false or inaccurate information regardless of intentional authorship" (Southwell et al.)
estimates.source_quote: half—91 (51.1%)—contained misinformation. Therefore, 11.4% of the sample overall
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two authors hand-coded pins by comparing claims with reputable sources: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (especially its herbs and botanicals guide), the World Cancer Research Fund, the National Cancer Institute, BreastCancer.org, Susan G. Komen, and published academic papers. Intercoder reliability from an 80-pin pretest coded by both researchers: Krippendorff's alpha 0.82 for presence of misinformation in the image, 0.82 for presence of misinformation in the text, 0.91 for phase, 0.88 for source, 0.80 for presence of conspiracy theory.
estimates.moderator_quote: We used the software program ParseHub (ParseHub, Toronto, ON, Canada) to search the terms "breast cancer" and "breast + cancer," on November 14, 15, and 16, 2018, for a total of 6 searches. We then used ParseHub to automatically scrape links to the pins. We collected a sample of 838 pins, similar to previous research.
estimates.notes: 91/797 = 11.4%, consistent with the stated percentage (the count 91 is verbatim from the abstract). This is the whole-corpus denominator and is the row to pool. breadth coded 'misleading' rather than 'false' because the misinformation category includes exaggerated claims (54.9% of misinformation pins), 'no evidence' claims (18.7%), outdated guidance (4.4%) and 'error by omission' (2.2%) alongside strictly inaccurate content (16.5%). denom_selection=curated because the corpus is a rank-truncated scrape of Pinterest search results, not a random or census sample of breast-cancer pins.

estimates.country: Not stated (Pinterest platform-wide; authors based in the USA and framed around US women)
estimates.measure_type: % of breast-cancer pins that made a factual claim about prevention or treatment that contained misinformation
estimates.value_raw: 91 (51.1%) of 178 pins making a factual claim
estimates.denominator: 178 of the 797 pins that made a factual claim about what social media users could do to prevent or treat breast cancer (22.3% of the corpus; the remainder were mostly inspirational messages and product promotions)
estimates.definition: A pin was coded as containing misinformation if at least one claim in its text or image was shown to be false by evidence from reputable breast-cancer information sources; only one false claim was required
estimates.misinfo_def: "false or inaccurate information regardless of intentional authorship" (Southwell et al.)
estimates.page_loc: Results, first paragraph (p. S301); count 91 given in Abstract (p. S300)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two authors hand-coded pins by comparing claims with reputable sources: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, the World Cancer Research Fund, the National Cancer Institute, BreastCancer.org, Susan G. Komen, and published academic papers. Krippendorff's alpha 0.82 for misinformation in image and 0.82 for misinformation in text (80-pin pretest, both researchers).
estimates.moderator_quote: This code captures whether each pin made a factual claim about what social media users could do to prevent or treat breast cancer. From the original sample of 797 pins, 178 (22.3%) met this criterion and were analyzed further. Excluded posts mostly consisted of inspirational messages and promotions for breast cancer–themed products.
estimates.notes: definition_variant=true: this is the same numerator (91 pins) over a narrower, screener-restricted denominator (claim-making pins only) than the 11.4% row. 91/178 = 51.1%, consistent. It is NOT within_misinfo_content: the 178 are pins making any factual claim, not a misinformation-only sample. Only one of these two rows should enter a pooled prevalence estimate; the 11.4% whole-corpus row is the natural choice.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) The location breakdown of misinformation (28.6% image only, 23.1% text only, 48.4% both), the misinformation-type breakdown (54.9% exaggerated, 18.7% no evidence, 16.5% inaccurate, 4.4% outdated, 2.2% contraindicated, 2.2% error by omission), the topical breakdown (39.6% foods, 19.8% vitamins/supplements, 9.9% environmental causes, 8.8% mammography, etc.), the phase breakdown (34.1% prevention, 41.8% treatment, 24.2% both) and the linked-source breakdown (71.4% blogs, 7.7% mainstream media, 3.3% medical sites, 5.5% other health sites, 2.2% social media, 2.2% other) are all computed WITHIN the 91 misinformation pins, so they describe the composition of misinformation rather than its prevalence and are not extracted as prevalence rows (they would be within_misinfo_content=true, appendix-only, and add nothing to the two rows above). (2) '95.6% of misinformation pins did not put forth any conspiracy theories' is likewise within the misinformation-only subsample and is a complement, not a prevalence share. (3) The 74% antivaccine figure for 800 vaccine pins is cited from Guidry et al. (reference 15), not this paper's own data, and is excluded by R8. (4) The 37% belief-in-FDA-cover-up figure is a belief measure cited from Oliver and Wood, both cited-from-elsewhere and belief-only, so excluded.

rob.design: Content analysis of pins scraped with ParseHub from six Pinterest searches ('breast cancer' and 'breast + cancer') run on 14-16 November 2018; 838 pins collected, 41 dead links dropped, 797 analysed; screen capture saved for each pin. Two-phase coding (deductive codebook then inductive typology). Both authors coded a random 80-pin pretest for reliability; the first author carried out subsequent coding alone. Krippendorff's alpha: 0.91 phase, 0.88 source, 0.82 misinformation in image, 0.82 misinformation in text, 0.80 conspiracy theory. Authors note the design cannot speak to diffusion or exposure: 'The mere presence of this misinformation on Pinterest does not guarantee that these pins were heavily viewed.' No country restriction, no engagement weighting, no random sampling of the platform.
rob.item6_quote: We determined the presence of misinformation by comparing the content of the pins to reputable sources of information on breast cancer, including the Web sites of the Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (especially its guide to herbs and botanicals21), the World Cancer Research Fund (especially its guide to diet, nutrition, and physical activity22), the National Cancer Institute,23 BreastCancer.org, Susan G. Komen,24 and published academic papers. If a claim in the pin was shown to be false by evidence from 1 of these sites, we coded the text or image in question as containing misinformation. Only 1 false claim was required to code for misinformation, even if the text or image made several claims.
rob.item10_quote: From the original sample of 797, 178 (22.3%) made a factual claim about what social media users could do to prevent or treat breast cancer. Of these, more than half—91 (51.1%)—contained misinformation. Therefore, 11.4% of the sample overall contained misinformation related to breast cancer prevention or treatment.
